body: The piano tuner finishes at twenty to five and the school hall behind him is empty — chairs stacked in sixes along the wall, the radiators ticking as they cool, one strip light left on above the stage because he cannot find the switch for the others. He takes out the felt wedges, lowers the lid, then sits down and plays for two minutes, because a piano is not finished until somebody has heard it as music rather than a series of intervals. Nobody hears it. Tomorrow three hundred children will sing over the top of it with the doors open, and it will never sound as good again as it does now, to nobody.

That is what a station sounds like before anyone is listening. The work is finished, correct and running, the room it is running into is empty, and the emptiness makes no difference whatever to how carefully it was done.

Every frequency on this band began in that condition. The catalogue was assembled, the schedule computed, the mount opened, the day file published — and for some stretch afterwards the number of people hearing it was none.

It is worth being precise about what runs during that stretch, because the word broadcast has quietly become a synonym for publishing. It is not one. A published thing sits still and waits to be asked for. A broadcast is already in progress. The schedule for a frequency is computed in advance and written out as a day file — every track, in order, with the second at which it starts — and the stream plays through it at real speed whether one person is connected or none. At three in the morning the fourth song of the evening block is not paused and not waiting. It is thirty-one seconds in, and if nobody joins for an hour then that song simply happened, in full, to nobody.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 assigned frequencies. Of those, 46 are on air. The rest are assigned and in build: numbers that exist, names that exist, formats and cover art that exist, and nothing yet coming out of them.

That is an expensive way to build. An hour of a silent frequency costs what an hour of a busy one costs — the same catalogue work, the same Scripture chosen under each track, the same check that the audio is the ministry’s own copy. There is no discount for obscurity, and the temptation to take one is constant, because nobody would find out. But a station that waits for an audience before deciding how good to be will be exactly as good as its first audience demands, and first audiences demand little. The audience arrives, if it arrives, long after the standard has been set.

This runs against nearly everything the surrounding culture believes about making things. The reigning wisdom is to ship the smallest version that works and let people’s behaviour tell you what to build — sensible for a checkout flow and quietly ruinous for anything meant to have a character. Character cannot be tested against a control group. It is the residue of decisions taken when they did not appear to matter, and learning from the audience postpones every one of them until there is an audience to have an opinion. By then the habits are the institution.

So the numbers here are committed before there is evidence that anybody wants them. HM 350.00 is The Upper Room, a prayer station, which opened this year on a number that had been set aside for it long before anybody asked for it. HM 393.10 is Grief Walked and HM 367.20 is Story Hour; both are assigned, and neither has opened yet. Each is a permanent commitment made on no data, which is the reverse of the sensible order and the only order in which anything with a name has been built. You cannot call people to a place that does not exist.
The alternative is perfectly respectable, and it deserves stating properly before it is taken apart.

Build nothing until somebody asks for it. Let demand decide, put the effort where the interest is, and you waste almost nothing; it is honest about uncertainty in a way grand plans are not, and it has produced a great deal of what people use. What it cannot do is serve anyone who was not already there to ask. A demand-led dial ends up with many stations in the languages that already have many and none in the ones that do not, because absence registers as lack of interest rather than lack of provision. And it will never open a frequency for the hour of the night when the people who need it most are awake, because those numbers look like an error.
Nothing improves once people are watching. It only becomes more visible.

The night desk at a small hotel in a Danish market town is a counter, a key rack, a card machine and a radiator that works if you kick it. It is ten past three; the rain has not let up since midnight, and one pair of shoes sits outside room fourteen. The porter is twenty-two and does this three nights a week around a course she is not sure about. She has closed the ledger, read everything on her phone twice, and put on a station in her own language — not for particular songs, but because she wanted something awake and Danish that was not aimed at her. It has been running for months. She is very probably the only person on that frequency in that hour in that country, and it does not sound like a station playing to one person. It sounds like a station playing.
Not one second of that hour was arranged for her. The standard she walked into was set months earlier by people with no idea she existed, and could not have been raised for her arrival.

The cost of this is real and should be said plainly rather than dressed up as patience. A great deal of careful work goes into hours nobody hears, and none of it comes back. HM 330.90 is West Africa Inspire, in Yorùbá, assigned and not yet on air; when it opens it will not trouble anybody’s figures, and it costs what a popular station costs. Meanwhile it is a number with silence behind it, which from outside looks less like patience than like a promise nobody kept.

But the silence is not a defect in the band. It is the band being honest about the order in which the work happens. Every frequency playing tonight was a silent number first, and the ones silent now sit in precisely the state the good ones were in when nobody could have told the difference. A dial showing only its finished stations would conceal the one stretch in which anything is genuinely decided. The unfinished half is not an embarrassment. It is the evidence.

So the test of a broadcaster is not what it does once it has an audience. It is what it did in the long stretch before — whether the schedule was still filled properly, whether the check still ran on a wet Tuesday in February, whether the Scripture under each song was still chosen carefully by somebody who knew nobody would notice if it were not. That stretch is where a station acquires whatever it is ever going to have.
All of that is arguable in the abstract and settled in four minutes by listening to one.

The dial is in two states at once and does not hide which is which. Part of it is on air and playing at this moment — the flagship, the worship and gospel formats, the late-night stations, the ones for children, and one frequency per language for the nations. The rest is assigned and in build. HM 375.80 is Inspire Rising, for new artists, assigned and still silent. HM 365.40 Stillwater and HM 300.30 Inspire Hymns & Heritage are likewise assigned and not yet on air. All of them show on the dial, which is deliberate — a band listing only its live frequencies would be telling you a smaller, more flattering truth about itself.

If you want the finished version of everything above, put on HM 324.20 — Danmark Inspire, in Danish. It is on air tonight and it is the plainest case on the band of a station with no incentive whatever to perform. Danish will never be the largest number here; at four in the morning in Jutland that frequency is close to empty, and it plays a full, properly built schedule into the emptiness regardless. Tune to it from wherever you are and you will not understand a word, which is very nearly the point: with the language out of reach you are left listening to what this article has been about, which is care taken in a room that is mostly not there. It was a silent number once too — named, assigned, in build, waiting.

Nothing needs installing to do that. No app, no download, no card: open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play. The player is built for inexpensive handsets and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people own, and if you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else there. Do make yourself an account while you are on it. It is free, it carries your favourites across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for — which is how the silent numbers get chosen, built and opened.

Then leave it running. That is the whole of the instruction — no evaluating and no exploring, because the tuner in the empty hall was not being evaluated either and the music was still the best thing in the building. Put HM 324.20 on tonight while you are doing something else, and let it play to you the way it has been playing to almost nobody for months. If the standard holds in an empty room, you can be fairly confident what it will do in yours.
